Tadpole madtom Noturus gyrinus is a diminutive ictalurid catfish that inhabits slow-moving, low-gradient streams and vegetated lake margins of eastern North America. Field collections from across its range indicate that individuals rarely exceed a total length of 13 cm [Li = 13 cm], a size that positions this species among the smallest members of its genus. At the onset of gonadal maturation, males and females have been measured at a total length of approximately 6.33 cm [Lp = approximately 6.33 cm], a figure converted from a standard length of 5 cm documented in reproductive assessments. The wet weight at birth, derived from the egg diameter of 2.96 mm, yields a hatchling mass of about 0.0136 grams [Wwb = about 0.0136 grams], an extraordinarily low value consistent with the small egg size typical of this species.

Laboratory studies conducted under controlled thermal conditions at 18 °C [T = 18 °C] have provided critical insights into the reproductive and life-span parameters of tadpole madtom. At this temperature, the maximum expected lifespan is approximately 4 years [am = approximately 4 years], a duration that aligns with the fast-paced life history of small, short-li at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]ved ictalurids. The maximum reproductive rate for females held at 18 °C [T = 18 °C] was derived from an estimated annual fecundity of 61 offspring [Ri = annual fecundity of 61 offspring] produced over the course of a single spawning season, yielding an average of approximately one offspring every six days. This annual [F_R_i = annual] reproductive output reflects the species’ strategy of producing a modest number of eggs per spawning event, with females likely depositing a single clutch per year in the wild.

The allometric relationship between length and body mass in Noturus gyrinus yields a predicted ultimate wet weight of 25.4 grams [Wwi = 25.4 grams] for a 13 cm individual, consistent with the slender, elongated body plan typical of benthic-dwelling madtoms. Correspondingly, the wet weight at puberty, estimated at the point of sexual maturation under standard conditions, is approximately 2.79 grams [Wwp = approximately 2.79 grams], based on the same length–mass relationship applied to the observed size at maturity. This marked increase from the 0.0136 gram [Wwb = 0.0136 gram] hatchling mass to the pubertal weight represents a greater than 200-fold gain, highlighting the rapid somatic growth that characterizes the early life stages of this species before reproductive investment begins.

Ecological studies have demonstrated that tadpole madtom exhibits a seasonal, single-clutch reproductive strategy typical of many small ictalurids. Females reach sexual maturity at a total length near 6.33 cm [Lp = 6.33 cm], though some field-caught specimens have been recorded maturing at a standard length of approximately 5 cm, suggesting that local environmental conditions and resource availability may modulate the precise size at which puberty is attained. Once mature, individuals can achieve a total length up to 13 cm [Li = up to 13 cm], with the largest females weighing as much as 25.4 grams [Wwi = 25.4 grams]. The onset of first reproduction in this species is tightly linked to water temperature, with spawning activity typically initiating in late spring or early summer when stream temperatures approach 18 °C [T = 18 °C].

Comparative analyses within the genus Noturus reveal that N. gyrinus possesses a relatively compressed life cycle, with a maximum longevity of 4 years [am = 4 years] when maintained at 18 °C [T = 18 °C] in a laboratory setting. Under these same thermal conditions, females produce a single annual clutch containing up to 61 eggs [N_R_i = clutch containing up to 61 eggs], and the reproductive rate is constrained to one spawning event per year [F_R_i = one spawning event per year]. The most extreme documented size for an adult tadpole madtom is 13 cm [Li = 13 cm] total length, corresponding to an asymptotic body mass of 25.4 grams [Wwi = 25.4 grams]. This combination of early maturation at roughly 6.33 cm [Lp = roughly 6.33 cm] total length and a relatively modest adult body size reflects an adaptive strategy for exploiting temporally stable but spatially restricted microhabitats in low-gradient streams and backwater pools.
